open_obligations: Do not transfer compute ratios between the two settings; Hammond and Adam-Day vary verifier width and number of layers, not compute ratio.
Check whether Hammond et al. saw instability with very small verifiers.
Note different protocols (checkability training versus nip).

Note that benefit is measured differently: Hammond and Adam-Day measure verifier capability gained over interacting with a random prover, while Kirchner et al. measure training stability, prover legibility and verifier robustness, and cannot exclude non-optimal hyperparameters as the cause of the poor performance of very small and large verifiers.
out.other_title: Checkability training works for mid-range verifier size; fails if too weak or prover-sized
out.rationale: Kirchner et al. report checkability training works for verifiers 10^-3 to 10^-1.8 of prover compute, but 10^-4 verifiers make training unstable and prover-sized verifiers do not become robust. Hammond and Adam-Day report on graph isomorphism that verifiers gain capability by interacting with a non-random prover rather than a random one, and that this gain is most pronounced for verifiers which cannot solve the task alone but can after learning to interact with the prover; the settings (checkability training with verifier size as a fraction of prover compute, versus nip on a graph isomorphism task with verifier width and number of layers varied) differ greatly.
out.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: how weak a verifier can be and still benefit from prover-verifier training

text: Varying the verifier's width and number of layers under nip, the paper reports that larger models can solve the task while smaller ones cannot, and that verifiers interacting with a trained (non-random) prover gain capability relative to interacting with a random prover. The gap is most pronounced for verifiers that cannot solve the task by themselves but can after learning to interact with the prover.
title: Weak verifiers gain most from interacting with a trained prover (nip, graph isomorphism)
